title: How a Reading Works

spine.markdown: Intertext is designed to support multiple texts. For the prototype we have adapted a text previously published in print, The Digital Plenitude (Bolter 2019).

The scrollable text is located in the left pane, while the right panes present an expandable table of contents and a space for the reader to type questions or comments. The text is presented in assimilable units of about 250 words each. The reader is invited to respond, after which the system responds with another unit tailored specifically to reader’s questions or comments. The reader may choose to respond again or to continue to the next section or to any other section or chapter.

Unlike most of the current reading systems, Intertext is envisioned for new texts or texts specifically adapted by their author for digital redefinition. Each Intertext begins from a base text, which is divided into sections and summarized to constitute the spine of the interactive version. In responding to a reader, the model draws first on the spine to guide its response. It may also draw on a fund of extra interpretive or factual units as well as a list of verified citations and a set of illustrative images and videos. The model can also search the web for further information.

Intertext’s responses are generated by prompting Claude Sonnet 5.5. Each prompt is a bundle consisting of summaries of the argument and previous reader responses together with fixed rules for responding. Claude’s initial completion is then revised for style before being delivered to the reader. The two passes are designed:

- To ensure that the responses do not exhibit random drift from the base argument.
- To maintain the tone as close as possible to the author’s text and limit stylistic tics of LLMs.
- To regulate the citation of outside works from a verified library of references.

fundEntries.title: Three ways to enter
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how a reading begins, what contributing means, or whether the original can still be read.
fundEntries.markdown:
Before reading begins, the reader makes one choice among three paths. Contribute means reading the evolving edition and
allowing the conversation to inform later versions. Read the current text gives the same edition with nothing saved.
Read the original gives the untouched authored text, without any reader's changes. The choice is made once, and there
is no view that compares editions during a reading.

fundEntries.title: The boxed opening and the Return key
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the boxed passage is, what pressing Return does, or how a section ends.
fundEntries.markdown:
Each section opens with a short boxed passage written for the reader: a scene and the section's thesis in brief. A
reader can then type a message, which gets an answer, or press Return with nothing typed, which carries the reading on
with the next ideas the text holds. The first Return treats the box as a prologue and begins at the first passage;
later Returns resume from where the conversation has reached. When a section's material is exhausted the text signals
completion, and a further Return moves to the next section.

fundEntries.title: Moving between sections
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether they can skip around, or how the text remembers what was said earlier.
fundEntries.markdown:
The contents list stays on screen, and the reader can move to any section at any time. Each section keeps its own
conversation. The text also keeps a short private summary of each section the reader has visited, so that a long
reading keeps its continuity without sending the whole transcript with every turn.

fundEntries.title: The look of the page
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks about the design of the reading page or why it looks like a book.
fundEntries.markdown:
The reader's page takes the form of an annotated book. The reading is set as a printed page in a Garamond typeface,
with red small capitals for labels and a drop cap opening each section. The reader's own words stand in the margin
beside the reply they drew, in italic, tied to it by a leader line, much as a reader's notes stand beside a printed
text; on narrow screens they stand above the reply instead. The contents and the input sit on a dark column to the
right.

fundEntries.title: What the spine is
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the spine contains, or whether the reader ever sees the author's text itself.
fundEntries.markdown:
The spine is the author's own text for the section, divided into passages, each with a stable identifier. It is the
authoritative route through the section, but the reader never sees it as such. When the reader presses Return, the
text retells the next passages in order, closely and often in the author's phrasing, compressed and joined to what
the conversation has already said. When the reader asks a question, the text draws on whatever in the spine bears on
it and answers in new words.

fundEntries.title: Why each section also has a statement of its argument
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks why the text needs summaries of the argument when it already holds the full text, or what keeps replies on course.
fundEntries.markdown:
Besides the spine, each section and each larger division of the work carries a short statement of its argument,
written or approved by the author and never shown to the reader. The full text supplies the material; the statement
supplies the direction. A section's text gives a passing example and its thesis roughly equal weight, and a model
answering a question about a detail tends to follow the detail. The statement tells it what is central. It steers
every reply, and it is stated only when the reader's message bears on it, in fresh words, as a claim.

fundEntries.title: Why a spine and a fund
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks why the material is split into a spine and a fund, or why readers' additions do not simply go into the text.
fundEntries.markdown:
A section is not one string that is rewritten and enlarged. Additions written by a model can be intelligent and
supportive and still damage the balance and rhythm of a continuous essay, because a model tends to apply an argument
to more cases and add more qualifications whether or not they belong in the main movement. So the concise route
through the section, the spine, is kept apart from optional material, the fund, which the text may select for a
particular reader at a particular moment.

fundEntries.title: What the fund holds
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what goes into the fund or how the text decides to use it.
fundEntries.markdown:
A fund entry is one of six kinds: a clarification, an example, a qualification, a counterargument, evidence or an
extension. Each is anchored to the passage it belongs with and carries a short cue saying when it is useful. The fund
is not a checklist: the text offers an entry only where it helps the reader's question without damaging the movement
of the section, and leaving the fund unused is often right. Only entries accepted for publication ever reach readers.

fundEntries.title: How citations are controlled
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the text decides what it may cite, or how hallucinated references are prevented.
fundEntries.markdown:
For each section the text may cite only the works on that section's library list, each described with what it says
and its pages. When it draws on one, it writes a private marker with the work's identifier and pages; the server
checks the identifier and the pages against the list and drops anything not listed, and the page turns each surviving
marker into a numbered note with a full reference in Chicago author-date style. The list also says how each writer is
to be mentioned: introduced and then named, cited by note only, or, for the author's own work, stated as the work's own
thinking without a name.

fundEntries.title: Images and videos
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks how the text shows images or videos, or whether it can show one.
fundEntries.markdown:
A reply may show one item from the section's checked list of videos, images and web pages, by writing a private token
on a line of its own. The server keeps only listed items, one per reply. The page plays a video only when its
embedding has been checked, shows an image only when its licence has been cleared, with its credit beneath, and shows
anything else as a card that opens in a new tab. Each item on the list says when it is worth showing, and the list is
kept by a script that checks every item rather than from memory.

fundEntries.title: Searching the web
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks whether the text knows about recent events or can look things up.
fundEntries.markdown:
The text can search the web, at most five times in a turn, for what it does not hold: current events, recent work, or
an outside source the reader asks about. Names, dates and details in the author's text remain authoritative, and an
outside detail never alters them. Whatever the text draws from a search reaches the reader as a numbered note, so the
reply carries no list of links.

fundEntries.title: What the model is given
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what goes into the prompt, or how much of the text the model sees at once.
fundEntries.markdown:
Each reply begins as a call to the model whose prompt puts first what stays the same through a section: the
instructions for the voice, the rule for citations, the section's label, the argument in brief, the opening box, the
section's text and its library list. These are cached and reused from turn to turn. After them come what changes:
instructions for a Return turn, the images and media not yet shown, the writers already introduced, short summaries of
other sections the reader has read, and the fund entries on offer. The conversation so far in the section follows as
messages.

fundEntries.title: What the revision does
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks what the second pass changes, or why a reply needs revising at all.
fundEntries.markdown:
The second call receives the draft together with the argument in brief, everything the reader has been shown so far,
the section's text and the reader's words. It returns the reply revised so that it answers the question in its opening
paragraph, introduces anything the reader has not yet met, names people already met by surname alone, keeps each claim
at the strength its evidence allows, cuts praise of the reader and repetition of earlier replies, and stays within 250
words. It may add no ideas and must keep every citation and media marker in place; if it changes one, the draft is used
instead.

fundEntries.title: A single voice
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks who is speaking, whether a passage came from the author, a reader or the model, or how the text handles an objection.
fundEntries.markdown:
The text speaks as the work, in the third person, in the register of a serious discussion between equals. It does not
announce whether a sentence came from the author's text, a fund entry, an earlier reader or the model. It answers the
reader's question first and widens from there; it meets an objection as an essay does, granting in a plain clause what
the reader has right and narrowing a claim that was too broad; and it acknowledges a real factual error plainly. The
reader is assumed to know only what has been shown in the conversation.

fundEntries.title: Which models do the work
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader asks which models InterText uses, or how the parts of a reply are kept private.
fundEntries.markdown:
Replies, revisions and evolution all run on Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5.5. Because that model cannot be compelled to
answer through a structured tool, the text reports its private choices with markers in its prose: which fund entries
it used, whether the section is complete, and a private memory of the section so far. The server reads these markers
and removes them before the reply goes on to the revision, the citation checks and the reader.

changeSummary: Structural package of the DH2027 paper (H-001): one passage per paragraph of the paper, the paper's prose unchanged apart from its figure references. Fund entries drafted from the InterText documentation by a Claude session (2026-11-25), as candidates for Jay's approval.
